reviewBoundary: Three new complete junior practices: four four-choice written passages for junior2; a four-email thread and independent three-choice passage for junior3. Fictional cases, no invented research/statistics. Same-author evidence, message chronology and distractor review only.

units.title: Breakfast club and moving pictures
units.alignmentNote: Two complete written four-question passages for junior2 explicitly adapt the written-reading part of its source. Junior3 retains a four-email thread with five questions plus a separate five-question reading, all three-choice. No source prose copied.

materials.title: A quieter start
materials.text:
Our school opened a breakfast club in the dining room. I expected it to be mainly for students who had not eaten at home. There was toast and fruit, but food was not the only reason people came.

Some students arrived early because of the bus timetable. Before the club opened, they waited outside their classrooms. Others wanted a place to finish reading before lessons. A teacher was always present, and conversation was welcome, but loud music was not.

I helped twice a week. At first, I tried to persuade everyone to join a game after eating. One student politely refused three times. I thought he did not like the club. Then he explained that the quiet ten minutes with his book were the best part of his morning.

We changed our arrangement. Games stayed at one end of the room, while a small sign marked a quiet table at the other. Nobody had to explain why they chose either area. The student began arriving earlier and sometimes helped put the books away.

The club did not become two separate groups. People moved between the tables when they wanted. What changed was our idea of a good welcome. Inviting someone into a place did not mean deciding exactly how they should enjoy it. By leaving different ways to take part, we gave more students a reason to stay.

questions.prompt: Why did some students arrive before lessons?
options: They had to play a game before school
Their bus timetable brought them early
Their classrooms had no books
They had been told to avoid breakfast
questions.explanation: Bus timing is directly stated. Avoiding food, compulsory games and bookless classrooms are not given reasons.

questions.prompt: Why did one student keep refusing the game?
options: He could not enter the dining room
He valued quiet time to read
He was waiting for loud music
He wanted the club to close
questions.explanation: He explicitly values reading. He attends the room and the club prohibits loud music; closure is not his aim.

questions.prompt: What did the organisers change?
options: They provided both a game area and a quiet table
They served food only to students who played
They required written reasons for sitting quietly
They removed every game from the room
questions.explanation: Two areas offer choice without explanation. Games remain and food is not tied to playing.

questions.prompt: What did the narrator learn about welcoming people?
options: A successful club makes everyone do the same thing
Food should be removed from a breakfast club
Different people may need different ways to participate
Quiet students should be asked to leave
questions.explanation: The final paragraph states inclusion through choices. Uniform activity and excluding quiet readers contradict the change; removing breakfast is never proposed.

materials.title: A small book that seems to move
materials.text:
Draw a ball near the bottom of one page, then draw it a little higher on the next. Continue across several pages, changing its position slightly each time. When the pages are turned quickly in order, the separate drawings can seem to form a moving ball. That is the basic idea of a flipbook.

The drawings do not need to be detailed. In fact, a simple shape is often easier for a beginner to keep consistent. What matters is how one image changes into the next. If the ball suddenly becomes much larger for no reason, viewers may notice the change in size instead of the movement you intended.

The spacing between positions affects the impression. Small changes can suggest slower movement, while larger changes can suggest a faster one, provided the sequence is still easy to follow. A jump that is too large may make the ball appear to vanish and return elsewhere.

It helps to test a few pages before drawing the whole sequence. Hold the pages at the same edge each time and practise turning them smoothly. A drawing placed too close to the held edge may be difficult to see.

A flipbook is a small project, but it shows how a planned series of still images can create an impression of action. Making one also gives beginners a reason to look closely at an ordinary movement they might otherwise take for granted.

questions.prompt: What is the main idea of a flipbook?
options: A sequence of still drawings can create apparent movement
The book needs electronic parts to work
One detailed drawing becomes a real object
Pages must contain only written instructions
questions.explanation: Rapidly ordered images suggest motion. Nothing becomes real, writing alone is not the method and no electronics are required.

questions.prompt: Why may a simple shape help a beginner?
options: It guarantees that every page turns automatically
It is easier to keep consistent across pages
It makes the held edge disappear
It removes the need for more than one drawing
questions.explanation: Consistency is the stated advantage. A sequence and manual turning are still needed; edges remain.

questions.prompt: What can happen if the ball’s position changes too much between pages?
options: It may seem to disappear and reappear
The pages must change colour
Every drawing becomes clearer
It will always move more slowly
questions.explanation: An excessive jump can look like vanishing/reappearing. Slow movement comes from small spacing; clarity and colour change are not effects stated.

questions.prompt: Why should makers test a few pages first?
options: To make the book’s paper heavier
To avoid drawing any further pages
To prove that detailed drawings are impossible
To check visibility and smooth turning before completing the sequence
questions.explanation: Testing reveals placement and handling issues before full work. It does not prohibit detail, eliminate completion or change paper weight.

materials.title: Not a solo performance
materials.text:
I joined a beginner's dance class with my friend Rowan. We practised the steps separately at home, and I could complete my part without thinking very hard. At our next lesson, however, moving together was much more difficult.

Whenever Rowan hesitated, I tried to pull us into the next step. That made him lose his balance. I thought I was helping us stay on time. Our teacher asked us to stop and walk through the pattern slowly, without music.

She explained that a partner was not a piece of equipment to move into position. Each person needed enough information and space to respond. I had been looking mainly at my own feet, so I often noticed Rowan's difficulty only after I had already moved.

We tried again. I kept the steps small and paid attention to where he was. Rowan also told me when my movement was unclear. We made fewer dramatic gestures, but the pattern began to feel more connected.

At the end, the teacher played the music again. We still missed a turn, then smiled and continued from the next familiar step. Nobody applauded; it was an ordinary practice lesson. Yet I felt more satisfied than after my faultless rehearsals alone. I had begun to understand that doing my part correctly was only one part of doing something together.

questions.prompt: What had the narrator practised at home?
options: A performance before an audience
Every movement with the teacher
The narrator’s own steps separately
Only listening without moving
questions.explanation: Home practice was separate steps. Teacher-led partner work happens in class, and no audience or movement-free practice is described.

questions.prompt: Why did pulling Rowan forward cause trouble?
options: It reduced his chance to respond and upset his balance
It removed every difficult turn
It gave him too much space
It made the music stop permanently
questions.explanation: The pull unbalances Rowan; the teacher explains response and space. It does not stop music or erase turns, and it restricts rather than increases his control.

questions.prompt: What changed in the second attempt?
options: Rowan was told never to speak
They stopped learning the pattern
Both partners gave information and the narrator watched Rowan more
The narrator used larger movements to force the pace
questions.explanation: The narrator attends to Rowan and Rowan explains unclear cues. Silence, forcing and abandoning the pattern contradict this.

questions.prompt: Why was the narrator pleased at the end?
options: Rowan no longer needed to take part
They were learning to coordinate rather than just perform individual steps
Their teacher promised a competition prize
They had completed a flawless public performance
questions.explanation: The ending contrasts coordinated practice with perfect solo steps. There is no public show, prize or removal of the partner.

materials.title: A fridge for the neighbourhood
materials.text:
A community centre in our town runs a shared fridge. Local food shops and residents may offer suitable food that would otherwise go unused. Visitors can take items without payment, but the fridge is not simply a place to leave anything from a kitchen.

Volunteers check donations against the centre's written rules. Food must be within its use-by date where one is given, and certain items are not accepted. The rules also explain packaging and temperature requirements. A volunteer who is unsure sets an item aside and asks the coordinator rather than guessing.

Each morning, the team checks that the fridge is operating correctly and cleans the storage area. They arrange items so that dates and labels can be seen. A full fridge is not helpful if people cannot tell what is inside a container or whether it has been stored properly.

Visitors are asked to take what they expect to use. They do not have to explain their personal circumstances or prove that they deserve a particular item. A notice gives the opening hours and the coordinator's contact details for anyone who wants to help.

The project reduces some waste, but it also depends on regular work. Donating food is only the beginning of making it available. Checks, clear information and respect for the people using the service are part of the arrangement too.

questions.prompt: What do volunteers do if uncertain about a donation?
options: Require a visitor to test it
Place it in the fridge without checking
Change its use-by date
Ask the coordinator rather than guess
questions.explanation: The rules require setting aside and seeking advice. Unchecked placement, altered dates and visitor testing are not allowed procedures.

questions.prompt: Why are dates and labels kept visible?
options: To avoid cleaning the fridge
To make every item look newly cooked
So volunteers can hide what each container holds
So visitors can understand the stored food and its information
questions.explanation: Visibility supports informed use. It is the opposite of hiding and does not change freshness or remove cleaning.

questions.prompt: What must visitors explain before taking food?
options: No personal justification is required
How much money they have
Why they deserve each item
Their complete family history
questions.explanation: The passage explicitly rejects personal proof. Family history, deservingness and financial details are not required.

questions.prompt: What is the writer’s main point?
options: Volunteers should judge the worth of each visitor
A useful shared fridge needs checks and ongoing organisation as well as donations
A full fridge never needs information or cleaning
Any food becomes suitable as soon as it is donated
questions.explanation: The conclusion states the broader work. Other options deny safety/organisation or contradict respectful access.

materials.title: Four emails about a repair afternoon
materials.text:
Email 1 — Monday, 3 March, 09:00
From: Ms Chen
To: Student Helpers
Subject: Saturday repair afternoon
The community repair afternoon is planned for Saturday, 8 March, in the west hall. Visitors will bring small household items for qualified volunteers to inspect. Student helpers will welcome visitors and explain the queue. Please arrive at 12:30 for a briefing; doors open at 13:00. Do not attempt repairs yourselves. Reply by Wednesday if you can help.

Email 2 — Tuesday, 4 March, 16:00
From: Daniel
To: Ms Chen
Subject: Re: Saturday repair afternoon
I can help, but my music lesson ends at 12:30. I could reach the centre by 13:00. Should I still come, or would missing the briefing mean I cannot take part? I am happy to do a later job if that is more useful.

Email 3 — Wednesday, 5 March, 10:00
From: Ms Chen
To: Student Helpers
Subject: Updated room and briefing
The west hall's heating has failed, so we will use the east hall. The event date and public opening time are unchanged. I will give the main briefing at 12:30 and repeat it for late helpers at 13:15. Daniel and anyone else arriving after 12:30 should wait at the welcome desk until the repeat briefing. Please do not start directing visitors before hearing the instructions.

Email 4 — Friday, 7 March, 14:00
From: Ms Chen
To: Student Helpers
Subject: One final reminder
Please use the side entrance nearest the east hall. The main entrance will be reserved for visitors carrying items. Wear your school badge. We have enough helpers for the queue, but need two people to put chairs away at 16:00. Reply to this email if you can stay for that task. Thank you for supporting the qualified repair volunteers.

questions.prompt: What is the student helpers’ planned role?
options: Inspect electrical items without supervision
Welcome visitors and explain the queue
Promise that every item can be repaired
questions.explanation: Email1 assigns welcome and queue roles while explicitly prohibiting repairs. No guarantee of repair is given.

questions.prompt: Why does Daniel write his email?
options: To announce that the whole event is cancelled
To ask whether he can help after missing the first briefing
To request an earlier music lesson from Ms Chen
questions.explanation: He explains timing and asks about later participation. He neither cancels the event nor asks Ms Chen to alter his lesson.

questions.prompt: Which arrangement changes on Wednesday?
options: The hall used for the event
The Saturday event date
The 13:00 public opening time
questions.explanation: Email3 changes west to east hall and explicitly preserves date and public opening time.

questions.prompt: What should Daniel do when he arrives at 13:00?
options: Look for the original briefing in the west hall
Wait at the welcome desk for the 13:15 briefing
Begin directing visitors immediately
questions.explanation: Late helpers must wait for the repeat briefing. Starting first violates instructions, and west hall has been replaced.

questions.prompt: Who should reply to Friday’s email?
options: Only students who can repair household items
Every visitor bringing a broken item
Helpers able to stay and put chairs away at 16:00
questions.explanation: The final email asks for two cleanup helpers to reply. Visitors are not its recipients and repairs are not the student role.

materials.title: Listening to the room
materials.text:
A piano tuner visited our school before a concert. I expected him to sit down, play a few notes and finish quickly. Instead, he first asked when the instrument had last been moved and whether the hall had been unusually warm or cold.

He explained that the piano was not separate from its surroundings. Conditions could affect the instrument, and moving it could change what needed attention. That did not mean every problem had the same cause. He needed to examine this piano rather than repair an imagined average one.

While he worked, I waited for him to play a complete tune. He mostly played small groups of notes, listening and adjusting. The repeated fragments sounded strange to me, but they gave him information that a familiar melody might distract us from noticing.

Afterwards, he let our music teacher try a piece. She asked about one passage, and he listened again. There was no dramatic announcement that the piano had become perfect forever. It was ready for the concert, with advice about its care and a reminder to report further changes.

I had thought expertise would look like instant certainty. What I saw was a sequence of precise questions, focused listening and small decisions. The tuner did not know less because he examined the circumstances. His knowledge helped him recognise which circumstances were worth examining.

questions.prompt: What surprised the narrator at the beginning?
options: The tuner asked about the piano’s circumstances before adjusting it
The piano had been removed from the school
The tuner refused to enter the hall
questions.explanation: He first asks about movement and temperature. No refusal or removal is described.

questions.prompt: What does “an imagined average one” refer to?
options: A generic piano treated without considering this instrument’s situation
The school’s actual concert programme
A particular tune the teacher wanted to play
questions.explanation: The phrase contrasts individual diagnosis with generic assumptions. It does not describe the programme or a piece of music.

questions.prompt: Why did the tuner play short groups of notes?
options: They helped him hear details relevant to adjustments
He was unable to play any note correctly
He wanted to prevent the teacher from listening
questions.explanation: The fragments provide focused information. Incompetence and exclusion are not suggested.

questions.prompt: What did the tuner claim after finishing?
options: The piano was prepared for the concert and needed ongoing care
It would remain perfect forever
No future change should ever be reported
questions.explanation: Readiness plus care advice and reporting are explicit. Permanent perfection and ignoring changes are rejected.

questions.prompt: How did the narrator’s view of expertise change?
options: It became the ability to avoid all questions
It came to include asking precise questions about the particular situation
It required making a dramatic promise every time
questions.explanation: The conclusion values targeted inquiry and decisions. Avoiding questions and dramatic guarantees contradict the observed expertise.
